To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we developed a novel auditory brain–computer communication system based on a natural stimulus, human speech, which has been successfully evaluated with healthy volunteers.
we have developed a novel auditory BCI that is based on a dichotically presented human voice and that has been evaluated with a group of healthy participants.
we have developed an auditory BCI that can be operated by people with complete locked-in syndrome, and that we have shown that it is possible to communicate with these patients using this interface.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a new BCI paradigm based on natural speech stimuli, which can be used to provide a more natural and intuitive communication with users unable or unwilling to use visual BCI paradigms.

the development of a fully auditory BCI that is able to interact with users using only their voice as a stimulus, thus avoiding the need of any muscular activity, and thus being suitable to be used by locked-in patients or patients under unresponsive wakefulness state.
the development of novel auditory EEG-based BCIs, with the aim of improving the usability and the performance of these interfaces.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the auditory BCI is a promising tool for communication with locked-in patients and for the rehabilitation of patients with severe motor impairment.
the results of the present work demonstrate the feasibility of an EEG-based auditory BCI that can be used to transmit information to a user without visual feedback.
this is the first auditory BCI that uses the dichotic listening paradigm and human voices for stimulation, with promising results for the future.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
this auditory BCI is a promising tool for patients with severe motor impairment, such as patients with complete locked-in syndrome, who cannot use visual BCIs.
we have developed a novel auditory BCI based on a dichotical listening paradigm using human voices as stimuli that has been tested with healthy volunteers.

we have developed an auditory BCI based on a dichotically presented speech stimulus, that is, a voice stimulus presented simultaneously to both ears, with the voice being heard by the subject from the ear on the right hemisphere, and not heard from the ear on left hemisphere.
The main takeaway from our work is that
auditory BCIs can be a viable alternative to the current visual BCIs, especially when the user has no muscular control.

auditory BCIs based on dichotic listening can be used to communicate with people with complete locked-in state, as well as with people with unresponsive wakefulness, and with other patients who are unable to communicate using a visual interface.

the auditory modality is a viable and promising approach to the development of BCIs, which could be of particular interest for patients with complete motor paralysis or in an unresponsive state, and for people with visual impairments.
